The '''Wellington Monument''' is a {{convert|175|ft|m|adj=mid|-high}} triangular [[obelisk]] located on a point of the [[Blackdown Hills National Landscape|Blackdown Hills]], {{convert|3|km|abbr=in}} south of [[Wellington, Somerset|Wellington]] in the English county of [[Somerset]]. It is a grade II* [[listed building]] and is the tallest three-sided obelisk in the world.<ref name=nhle>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1060281 |desc=Wellington Monument|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref>

The monument was designed to commemorate the [[Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington|Duke of Wellington's]] victory at the [[Battle of Waterloo]]. Construction of the original design commenced in 1817; a revised and cheaper design was eventually used, though, and building was completed in 1854. It is now owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]], which closed the monument to the public in 2007, owing to safety concerns;<ref name=projectupdate/> surveys showed that extensive renovation work was needed. Repairs were completed, leaving the monument "now possibly in better condition than when it was first completed" and the monument reopened in August 2021.<ref name=repairs2021/>

==Construction==

The monument was erected to celebrate the victory of [[Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington]], at the 1815 [[Battle of Waterloo]]. Following his victory at the [[Battle of Talavera]] in 1809, Wellesley was [[ennobled]] as a [[viscount]]. [[Peerages in the United Kingdom]] usually include a [[territorial designation]], symbolically tying them to a particular location. Because Arthur was abroad with the army, his brother [[Richard Wellesley, 1st Marquess Wellesley|Richard Wellesley]] selected the location; he chose the town of [[Wellington, Somerset]], due to its similarity to the family name, although Arthur Wellesley had never visited it. The new title was 'Viscount Wellington of Talavera, and of Wellington in the County of Somerset'.<ref name="gazette">{{London Gazette |issue=16291 |date=26 August 1809 |page=1342 }}</ref> Parliament awarded him £100,000, and with this he bought two [[Manorialism|manors]] in the town, including the land the monument now stands on. The association was continued with Wellesley's subsequent promotions to higher ranks of nobility; he ultimately became [[Duke of Wellington (title)|Duke of Wellington]] in 1814.<ref name="Elliott">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ywM9AAAAYAAJ&pg=PR13|title=The Life of the Most Noble Arthur, Duke of Wellington|last=Elliott|first=George|year=1816|publisher=J.Cundee|location=London |page=xiii–xiv}}</ref>

The monument was proposed in 1815 by William Sanford of [[Nynehead Court]], and he started a public subscription to pay for it. Within months £1450 had been raised and a design competition was held. The winning entry envisaged a {{convert|95|ft}} pillar with three cottages at the base to house old soldiers as caretakers. It was designed by [[Thomas Lee (1794–1834)|Thomas Lee]] and the foundation stone was laid by [[Lord Somerville]] in 1817.<ref name=everythingexmoor>{{cite web|title=Wellington Memorial Monument|url=http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=1046|publisher=Everything Exmoor|access-date=16 March 2014|archive-date=18 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160818001042/http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=1046|url-status=dead}}</ref>  By 1818 the column was {{convert|47|ft}} high but all funds had been spent. Another appeal raised further funds, and the column was raised to {{convert|121|ft}} by 1820. It was damaged in 1846 when it was struck by [[lightning]].<ref name=byford>{{cite book|last=Byford|first=Enid|title=Somerset Curiosities|date=1987|publisher=Dovecote Press|isbn=0946159483|pages=[https://archive.org/details/somersetcuriosit0000byfo/page/123 123–124]|url=https://archive.org/details/somersetcuriosit0000byfo/page/123}}</ref>

Construction restarted after the Duke's death, and was completed in 1854 by [[Henry Goodridge]].<ref name=nhle/> The monument's design was inspired by an Egyptian [[obelisk]], but in the shape of the [[Bayonet#Socket bayonets|type of bayonet]] used by Wellington's armies, a spike of triangular cross-section rather than a blade,<ref name="curio">{{cite book |title=Curiosities of Somerset |last=Leete-Hodge |first=Lornie |year=1985 |publisher=Bossiney Books |location=Bodmin |isbn=0-906456-98-3 |page=67 }}</ref> with funds raised from local subscribers to commemorate his achievements.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Wellington Monument of Somerset|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000187/18530120/025/0004|access-date=7 July 2014| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription |work=Bath Chronicle and Weekly Gazette|date=20 January 1853}}</ref> The initial designs envisaged a [[cast iron]] statue of the Duke on the top of the column with more statues on the plinth, but these were never built.<ref name=nhle/> The upper section of the column was restored in 1890 when the pinnacle was raised by {{convert|1.5|m|ft}}.<ref name=nhle/>

The original plans were for twenty-four cannons, captured from the [[Army of the North (France)|French army]] at the Battle of Waterloo, to be installed around the base.<ref name=nhle/> In 1818 one brass and 15 iron cannons were transported from the [[Royal Arsenal]] at [[Woolwich]] to [[Exeter Quay]], but they were never transported to the monument. After years of storage at [[Exeter]] ten were sunk into the ground as [[Bollard (traffic)|bollard]]s, and the brass gun sold in 1837 for £64 to cover the storage costs incurred by the local corporation. In 1890, when four guns were requested for the monument as part of a restoration project, they were found to be naval cannons cast in Scotland dating from 1789, and never used at the Battle of Waterloo.<ref name=byford/> Four cannons were eventually installed in 1910, surrounding the monument, but these were removed during the Second World War (1939–1945) for scrap metal to help the war effort.<ref name=everythingexmoor/> The need for scrap metal fell and they were eventually buried at [[Watchet]]. The one cannon remaining at Exeter was brought to the monument in 1977 and finally installed in 1984.<ref name=byford/>

==Architecture==
[[File:Monument Base (2480832440).jpg|thumb|left|The doorway at the base]]
The monument is built of local stone, Calcareous Grit, a [[Sandstone]] from [[Northay]].<ref name=everythingexmoor/> The triangular column is {{convert|80|ft|m}} wide at the base and {{convert|175|ft|m}} high.<ref name=nhle/> The base has an Egyptian winged panel above the studded iron door and is surmounted by a coved [[dentil]] [[cornice]].<ref name=nhle/>

A [[counterweight]] hangs inside the top of the monument to help balance it in windy weather. An internal staircase ascends to a viewing platform,<ref>{{cite web | title=Circular Walk Twelve – Wellington to the Monument | work=Taunton Deane Borough Council website | url=http://www.tauntondeane.gov.uk/irj/go/km/docs/CouncilDocuments/TDBC/Documents/Heritage%20and%20Landscape/Circular%20Walks/20061101WellyMonument.pdf | access-date=11 July 2014 | archive-date=14 July 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714220019/http://www.tauntondeane.gov.uk/irj/go/km/docs/CouncilDocuments/TDBC/Documents/Heritage%20and%20Landscape/Circular%20Walks/20061101WellyMonument.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref> which has three circular windows, one on each face.
{{clear}}

==National Trust ownership and restoration==

The monument was acquired by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1934.<ref name=repairs2021/><ref name=updown>{{Cite web |title=The ups and downs of Wellington Monument |author=<!--not stated--> |work=National Trust |date=<!--undated--> |access-date=27 August 2021 |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wellington-monument/features/the-ups-and-downs-of-wellington-monument}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Wellington Monument|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000514/19340127/147/0019|access-date=7 July 2014|work=Bath Chronicle and Weekly Gazette|date=27 January 1934| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is floodlit on special occasions with new lights installed in 2015. In 1985, the Wellington Rotary Club donated the cannon currently standing at the base of the monument.<ref name=everythingexmoor/>

The National Trust closed the monument to the public in 2007, owing to safety concerns.<ref name=projectupdate>{{cite web | title=Wellington Monument project update | publisher=National Trust | url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1355799880764/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224110013/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1355799880764/|archive-date=24 December 2013}}</ref> Surveys showed that extensive renovation work was needed to reopen the internal staircase to the viewing platform.
In June 2009, the National Trust announced plans to reclad the monument at a cost of £4 million.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/somerset/8102376.stm|title=Wellington monument to cost £4m|work=BBC News|publisher=BBC|access-date=16 June 2009 | date=16 June 2009}}</ref>

The painted fence was replaced by an open wire fence in 2010, aiding visibility, but still preventing public access to the base of the monument. Survey work in 2010 showed the extent of cracks in the stonework.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cameron|first=Alex|title=£50,000 on survey work at Wellington Monument|url=http://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/news/8352185.__50_000_on_survey_work_at_Wellington_Monument/|access-date=16 March 2014|newspaper=Somerset County Gazette|date=26 August 2010}}</ref> In 2013 it was announced that further funding would be needed for the restoration project.<ref>{{cite news|last=Marsh|first=Michael|title=No quick fix to Wellington Monument restoration, says The National Trust|url=http://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/news/10667296.No_quick_fix_to_Wellington_Monument_restoration__says_The_National_Trust/|access-date=16 March 2014|newspaper=Somerset County Gazette|date=12 September 2013}}</ref> Sensors recording the movement of the tower are also to be installed.<ref name=projectupdate/>

In 2015 [[Rebecca Pow]] the new local [[Member of Parliament]] for [[Taunton Deane]] asked the government to make available money for a restoration fund.<ref>{{cite web|title=MP calls for Wellington Monument restoration funds|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-33013996|website=BBC News|date=4 June 2015}}</ref> In 2016 she further highlighted the deteriorating condition of the monument and started a petition for its repair.<ref>{{cite web|title=MP launches petition to repair Wellington Monument|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-36330419|website=BBC News|date=19 May 2016}}</ref>

Complicated repairs were completed, over two years and at a cost of £3.1m, and the monument reopened in August 2021; the Trust said that after repairs it was expected to be removed from the at-risk register, and that it was "now possibly in better condition than when it was first completed".<ref name=repairs2021>{{Cite news |title=Duke of Wellington monument to reopen after £3.1m repairs |last=Brown |first=Mark |newspaper=The Guardian |date=27 August 2021 |url= https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2021/aug/27/duke-of-wellington-monument-to-reopen-to-visitors-after-repairs}}</ref>

6589393.title: Walton and Ivythorn Hills
6589393.extract:
Walton and Ivythorn Hills is a 34.9 hectares (86 acres) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest near Street at the south-eastern end of the Polden Hills in the English county of Somerset. Walton Hill is south of the village of Walton, and Ivythorn Hill is south of Street. Notified in 1953, the site is now owned and managed by the National Trust who acquired the freehold in 1988.
The hills which rise to 80 metres (260 ft) above Ordnance datum (mean sea level) are made up of limestone, rheatic clay and Keuper marl covered with calcareous grassland, scrubland and coppiced woodland. A quarry existed in the Middle Ages. This supports a variety of Butterflies, Leafhoppers, Spiders, Soldier Flies and Great Green Bush Crickets living on the vegetation. Notable buildings include Ivythorne Manor, which was originally built for Glastonbury Abbey, Walton windmill and a small sanatorium which became the first youth hostel in Somerset. In 1977 a short lived hippie camp was set up on Ivythorne Hill. The camp was a Free Festival to celebrate  7/7/77. The festival was attended by an estimated 3,000 people and was basically a one-day affair, with some people arriving early and the hangers on eventually evicted by the council.

'''Stembridge Tower Mill''' in [[High Ham]], [[Somerset]], England, is the last remaining [[thatched]] [[windmill]] in England. The mill is a grade II* [[listed building]].

The stone [[tower mill]] was built in 1822 with four floors and a thatched "cap". A [[steam engine]] was installed in 1894, and became the mill's sole source of power after a storm damaged it in 1897 or 1898. Commercial use ended in 1908. The mill is now owned by [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|The National Trust]]. In 2009, it underwent a £100,000 restoration by local craftsmen funded by the Grantscape Community Heritage Fund, and was re-opened later that year.

==History==
Stembridge Mill was constructed for Robert Tatchell in 1822.<ref name=Brown>{{cite book |title=Windmills of England |first=R. J. |last=Brown |publisher=Robert Hale Ltd |location=London |page=164 |year=1976 |isbn=978-0709156413}}</ref> It incorporated parts from the earlier Ham Mill,<ref name="coulthard">{{cite book |title=Windmills of Somerset and the men who worked them |last1=Coulthard |first1=Alfred J. |last2=Watts |first2=Martin |year=1978 |publisher=Research Publishing Co|location=London |isbn=978-0705000604 |pages=49–51 }}</ref> a few hundred yards to the north east.<ref name=Brown/> The mill has a {{convert|26|ft|m}} tower situated on an old mill mound,<ref>{{cite book|last=Warren|first=Derrick|title=Curious Somerset|year=2005|publisher=Sutton Publishing|location=Stroud|isbn=978-0-7509-4057-3|page=68}}</ref> surrounded by a low wall intended to keep people and livestock away from the sails.<ref name=greeves>{{cite book|last1=Greeves|first1=Lydia|title=History and Landscape: The Guide to National Trust Properties in England, Wales and Northern Ireland|date=2006|publisher=National Trust Books|isbn=978-1905400133}}</ref>

Tatchell leased the mill to his son-in-law John Sherrin, who inherited the mill in 1824 following Tatchell's death. When Sherrin died, the mill passed to his three sons, although only one, Robert, worked the mill. Simon Spearing became the miller in 1869. He was later assisted by his son William, who lost an arm when he was thirteen due to an accident at a [[watermill]] in [[Low Ham]].<ref name=Brown/> The mill was acquired by Adam Sherrin in 1881 and owned by his family until 1902.<ref name=natarchive>{{cite web |title=High Ham Deeds |url=https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/rd/dcea9991-3b2c-46d3-84f3-276169a77768 |publisher=National Archives |access-date=31 March 2015}}</ref> By the late 1880s, the mill was being rented by George Parker.<ref name=dunning/> He added a [[portable steam engine]] as auxiliary power.<ref name="coulthard"/> It drove one pair of stones. The mill was damaged by storms in 1897 or 1898 and after that was only powered by the steam engine, which had been installed in 1894, rather than the wind.<ref name=dunning>{{cite web|last1=Dunning|first1=Robert|title='High Ham', in A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 8, the Poldens and the Levels|url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/som/vol8/pp70-91#h3-0017|website=British History Online|publisher=Victoria County History|access-date=31 March 2015}}</ref> The bakehouse ceased to be used around this time.<ref name=Brown/>

Robert Hook then acquired the mill. Unable to compete against grain imports and the building of dockside mills at [[Avonmouth]], Stembridge Mill was last used commercially in 1908.<ref name=Brown/> Hook sold the mill and {{convert|5|acre|ha}} of land to Dr. Hugh Hale Leigh Bellot for [[Pound Sterling|£]]500. Upon his death in 1928,<ref name=Brown/> it was inherited by his son, Professor [[Hugh Hale Bellot]].<ref name=natarchive/> In 1969 Professor Bellot left the windmill, miller's cottage and garden to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in his will.<ref name=EH/> New sails were added in 1971, along with other repairs. Further repairs were carried out in 1974, including the removal of floors.<ref name=Brown/> It was designated as a grade II* [[listed building]] in 1986.<ref name=EH>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1235260 |desc=Stembridge Mill|access-date=4 April 2015}}</ref>

It is the last survivor of five windmills that once existed in the area.<ref name="curio">{{cite book |title=Curiosities of Somerset |last=Leete-Hodge |first=Lornie |year=1985 |publisher=Bossiney Books |location=Bodmin |isbn=978-0906456996 |page=84 }}</ref>

In 2009 the sails were replaced and the mill re-thatched and restored by local craftsmen at a cost of a £100,000; the mill was re-opened later that year. The work was funded by the Grantscape Community Heritage Fund.<ref>{{cite journal | title = The National Trust Magazine | journal = News | issue = Autumn 2009 | page = 11}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Thatched windmill sails again |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/local/somerset/hi/people_and_places/newsid_8308000/8308324.stm|publisher=BBC|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref> Although the sails do not rotate with the wind, they are moved 90 degrees four times per year for maintenance.<ref>{{cite news|title=Britain's only thatched windmill restored to former glory|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/6409038/Britains-only-thatched-windmill-restored-to-former-glory.html|access-date=31 March 2015|work=Telegraph|date=23 October 2009}}</ref> Before the restoration work was undertaken surveys revealed that the mill was used as a roost for [[Plecotus|long-eared]] and [[Horseshoe bat|lesser horseshoe bats]]. It was ensured that the bats would still have access after the restoration.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sails are returning to historic National Trust windmill|url=https://www.thisisthewestcountry.co.uk/news/4680054.Sails_are_returning_to_historic_National_Trust_windmill/|publisher=This is the West Country|access-date=31 March 2015}}</ref>

==Description==
''Note: Italicized terms are defined in the [[mill machinery]] article.''

Stembridge Mill is a [[tower mill]], a type of windmill which consists of a [[brick]] or stone tower, on top of which sits a roof or cap which can be turned to bring the [[Windmill sail|sails]] into the wind.<ref>{{cite web|title=Stembridge Tower Mill|url=http://windmills.org.uk/windmills/stembridge-tower-mill/|publisher=Windmills UK|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref> The advantage of the tower mill over the earlier [[post mill]] is that it is not necessary to turn the whole mill ("body", "buck") with all its machinery into the wind; this allows more space for the machinery and storage. In the earliest tower mills the cap was turned into the wind with a long tail-pole which stretched to the ground at the back of the mill. Later, a looping chain was used which turned the cap with gears, as is used at Stembridge.<ref name=greeves/> It is [[:wikt:wind#Verb|winded]] by a wheel and chain. The [[windshaft]] is of wood, with a cast iron cross, which carries four [[windmill sail#Common sails|common sails]]. The ''brake wheel'' is of clasp arm construction. No other machinery remains, since the ''wallower'', ''upright shaft'' and ''great spur wheel'' were removed after the mill ceased to operate by wind

The mill has four floors, a thatched cap and is constructed of local [[limestone]] known in the area as [[Blue Lias]].<ref name=dunning/> It has two pairs of {{convert|4|ft|m|2|adj=on}} diameter [[millstone]]s.<ref name="coulthard"/> One pair is French Burr stones, which date from 1859.<ref>{{cite web|title=Featured Mill ‒ Stembridge Mill, Somerset|url=http://wessexmillsgroup.org.uk/|publisher=Wessex Mills Group|access-date=31 March 2015}}</ref> The other pair has a French Burr runner stone on a conglomerate bedstone. Both pairs of millstones were originally driven ''overdrift'' by the windmill, with the mixed pair later being driven ''underdrift'' by the [[steam engine]], which also drove a wire machine.<ref name="coulthard"/> The remains of the old bakehouse can be seen at the rear of the mill.<ref name=greeves/>

==Millers==
The following millers worked Stembridge Mill:<ref name="coulthard"/><ref name=Brown/>
*John Sherrin (1822–?)
*Robert Sherrin (1861–69)
*Simon Spearing (1869–?)
*Joseph Loader (1879–81)
*George Parker (1889–97)
*Frank Parker (1897–98)
*Robert Mead (1898–?)
*F. G. Harding (post 1898)
*Mr. Hill (post 1898)

The '''Treasurer's House''' is a [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]-owned property in [[Martock]], in the English county of [[Somerset]]. It has been designated as a Grade I [[listed building]]. Apart from the [[Bishop's Palace, Wells]] it is the oldest house in the county.

The original 13th-century buildings have been added to several times, including a 15th-century great hall which has an arch-braced-collar truss roof. Several of the rooms have [[Mural|wall paintings]] which have been uncovered and restored since the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] were given the building in 1970. The house belonged to the [[Bishop of Bath and Wells]] and at one time was used to store the [[Great Seal of the Realm]] when [[John Langton (bishop of Chichester)|John Langton]] was the [[Lord Chancellor|chancellor]] of England.

==History==
The Treasurer's House is a [[Middle Ages|medieval]] priest's house built from [[Hamstone]] during the 13th century. The [[Solar (room)|solar block]], which was built around 1250 survives as the oldest part of the building,<ref>{{cite web|title=Martock Treasurer's House|url=http://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=2018|publisher=Britain Express|access-date=12 July 2015}}</ref> making it the second oldest inhabited house in Somerset.<ref name=martockonline>{{cite web|title=Treasurer's House|url=http://www.martockonline.co.uk/Pages/79/Treasurers-House.html|publisher=Martock Online|access-date=14 December 2013|archive-date=15 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215200158/http://www.martockonline.co.uk/Pages/79/Treasurers-House.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is mentioned as the parsonage attached to the village [[Church of All Saints, Martock|Church of All Saints]]. In 1227 it was acquired by [[Hugh of Wells]] the treasurer of [[Wells Cathedral]] who became the rector and patron of the church.<ref name=emery>{{cite book|last=Emery|first=Anthony|title=Greater Medieval Houses of England and Wales, 1300-1500, Volume 3|year=2006|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781139449199|page=589|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g7EXvaDEYioC&q=Treasurer%27s+House+Martock&pg=PA589}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Martock|url=http://www.martock.org/|publisher=Martock|access-date=14 December 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020015521/http://www.martock.org/|archive-date=20 October 2013}}</ref> The great hall was added in 1293.<ref name=martockonline/> In 1297 [[John Langton (bishop of Chichester)|John Langton]], who was a [[Lord Chancellor|chancellor]] of England and [[Bishop of Chichester]], received the [[Great Seal of the Realm]] which was stored at the "court at Martock".<ref name=baggs/> The kitchen was added in the 15th century.<ref name=nthouse/>

The [[Bishop of Bath and Wells|Bishop of Bath]] owned the building, which was known as Martock Priory, until 1849 when it was transferred to the [[Ecclesiastical Commissioners]].<ref name=baggs>{{cite web |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=117085 |title=Parishes: Martock |author=R.W. Dunning (editor), A.P. Baggs, R.J.E. Bush |publisher=Institute of Historical Research |date=1978 |work=A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 4 |access-date=14 December 2013 }}</ref> It was then privately owned and a small wing added. In 1943 it was bought by [[Harold St George Gray]], the librarian-curator of the [[Museum of Somerset|Museum]] for the [[Somerset Archaeological and Natural History Society]] to preserve it.<ref>{{cite news|title=Museums and Art Galleries|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000513/19430612/018/0004|access-date=16 April 2015|work=Western Daily Press|date=12 June 1943|page=4| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His wife bequeathed it to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1970.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=baggs/>

In 1987 it was designated as a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref name=nhle>{{NHLE | desc= The Treasurer's House | num=1225764 | access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref>

==Architecture==
[[File:Treasurers House and garden, Martock (geograph 2759000).jpg|thumb|left|The house and garden]]
The building has undergone various extensions and alterations since it was built.<ref>{{cite web|last=Richardson|first=Miranda|title=Martock|url=http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/Somerset_EUS_Martock.pdf|work=English Heritage Extensive Urban Survey|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=14 December 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214183252/http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/Somerset_EUS_Martock.pdf|archive-date=14 December 2013}}</ref> The building has a T-shaped plan, with the west projecting wing being a hall added in the late 13th century.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=emery/> The great hall has a 15th-century four-bay open arch-braced collar-truss timber roof.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=greeves>{{cite book|last1=Greeves|first1=Lydia|title=History and Landscape: The Guide to National Trust Properties in England, Wales and Northern Ireland|date=2006|publisher=National Trust Books|isbn=978-1905400133|page=391}}</ref> The roof was covered with slate from local quarries until it was thatched in the mid 19th century. The current clay tiles were used in the early 20th century.<ref name=emery/>

The kitchen block was added in the late 15th century or early 16th century and has no direct connection with the rest of the house.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=greeves/> The [[Solar (room)|Solar]] Block is the oldest part of the building dating from around 1250.<ref>{{cite web|title=Treasurer's House|url=http://www.stately-homes.com/treasurers-house|publisher=Stately-Homes.com|access-date=14 December 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20131214165141/http://www.stately-homes.com/treasurers-house|archive-date=14 December 2013}}</ref><ref name=nthouse>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/treasurers-house-martock/ |title=Treasurer's House |access-date=14 December 2013 |format= |publisher=National Trust }}</ref> It has a [[Tracery#Plate tracery|plate tracery]] window with a [[Trefoil arch|Trefoil]] cusping surrounded by [[Mural|wall paintings]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Penoyre|first1=Jane|title=Traditional Houses of Somerset|date=2005|publisher=Somerset Books|isbn=978-0861834075|page=103}}</ref> The solar separated from the hall by a [[screens passage]].<ref name=greeves/>

The walls of one of the private chambers on the upper floor were covered with 16th century [[Whitewash|limewash]] which was removed in 1995,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Papworth|first1=Martin|title=The Treasure beneath the Lime Wash|url=https://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/2013/06/02/926/|website=Archaeology National Trust SW|date=2 June 2013 |publisher=National Trust|access-date=12 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Russell|first1=Rosalind|title=Property: The family that's at home|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/money/property-the-family-thats-at-home-1276318.html|access-date=12 July 2015|work=Independent|date=1 February 1997}}</ref> to expose a 13th-century wall painting with a depiction of Jesus on the cross and two other figures.<ref>{{cite web|last=Papworth|first=Martin|title=The Treasure beneath the Lime Wash|url=https://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/tag/martock/|work=Archaeology National Trust SW|publisher=National Trust|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref> The crucifixion scene with rosettes and vine leaf decoration was uncovered in the 1990s.<ref name=emery/>

West Pennard Court Barn (which is also known as the Court Barn, West Bradley) is a late 14th or early 15th century tithe barn which was built for Glastonbury Abbey. The Grade I listed building is between West Pennard and West Bradley in the English county of Somerset.
The barn was restored by the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings in the 1930s following the collapse of the roof and then given to the National Trust. At 50 feet (15 m) long and 20 feet 6 inches (6.25 m) wide it is the smallest of the barns associated with the abbey. '''West Pennard Court Barn''' (which is also known as the '''Court Barn, West Bradley''') is a late 14th or early 15th century [[tithe barn]] which was built for [[Glastonbury Abbey]]. The Grade I [[listed building]] is between [[West Pennard]] and [[West Bradley]] in the English county of [[Somerset]].<ref name=nhle>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1175792 |desc=Court Barn|access-date=5 April 2015}}</ref>

The barn was restored by the [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]] in the 1930s following the collapse of the roof and then given to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]. At {{convert|50|ft}} long and {{convert|20|ft|6|in}} wide it is the smallest of the barns associated with the abbey. It has a [[cruck]] braced [[timber framing|timber framed]] roof and is supported by two-stage [[buttress]]es.

==History==
The barn which was originally known as Parson's Barn,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=117178 |title=Parishes: West Bradley |author=R. W. Dunning (editor), M. C. Siraut, A. T. Thacker, Elizabeth Williamson |publisher=Institute of Historical Research |year=2006 |work=A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 9: Glastonbury and Street |access-date=15 December 2013 }}</ref> was built on the orders of the Abbot of [[Glastonbury Abbey]] in the late 14th or early 15th century. There is no written record of the exact date and there is some debate about the likely age of the building based on the architectural features.<ref name=nt/><ref name=sher/> Along with several others barns it was used to collect the [[tithe]]s or dues to the abbey, often one tenth of a farm's produce. It fell within the [[Hundred (county division)|hundred]] of [[Glaston Twelve Hides]] which was named after the [[Hide (unit)|hides]] who gave [[Food render|food rent]] to [[Glastonbury Abbey]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Radford|first1=Courtenay Arthur Ralegh|last2=Abrams|first2=Lesley|last3=Carley|first3=James P.|title=The Archaeology and History of Glastonbury Abbey: Essays in Honour of the Ninetieth Birthday of C. A. Ralegh Radford |date=1991|publisher=Boydell & Brewer Ltd |isbn=9780851152844|page=63|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yB-0_rkhoBQC&q=West+Pennard+Court+Barn&pg=PA63}}</ref> The West Pennart Court Barn is the smallest of those which survive.<ref name=radford79>{{cite book|last1=Radford|first1=Courtenay Arthur Ralegh|last2=Abrams|first2=Lesley|last3=Carley|first3=James P.|title=The Archaeology and History of Glastonbury Abbey: Essays in Honour of the ninetieth birthday of C.A.Ralegh Radford|year=1991|publisher=Boydell Press|isbn=978-0851152844|pages=79–87|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yB-0_rkhoBQC&q=west+bradley+court+barn&pg=PA79}}</ref>

A survey in 1932 found that the roof was cracked and it eventually collapsed in 1935. In 1936 the roof structure was straightened, preserving the medieval [[truss]]es where possible, and covered with clay tiles.<ref name=garner>{{cite web|last1=Garner|first1=Keith|title=West Pennard Barn|url=http://www.kgarch.co.uk/projects/pennard/pennard.htm|publisher=Keith Garner Architects|access-date=18 May 2015|archive-date=16 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150116100204/http://www.kgarch.co.uk/projects/pennard/pennard.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> The restoration was undertaken by the [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]],<ref>{{cite web|title=West Pennard Court Barn|url=https://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3713|publisher=Britain Express|access-date=15 December 2013}}</ref> with the work being funded by Roger Clark of the local shoemakers [[C. & J. Clark]]<ref name=nt/> who bought the derelict barn for £5.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lovell|first1=Percy|title=Quaker inheritance, 1871-1961: a portrait of Roger Clark of Street based on his own writings and correspondence|date=1970|publisher=Bannisdale Press|page=224}}</ref> It has been owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 1938.<ref name=nt>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wra-1356292763044/view-page/item412748/ |title=West Pennard Court Barn |access-date=15 December 2013 |publisher=National Trust |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215221516/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wra-1356292763044/view-page/item412748/ |archive-date=15 December 2013 }}</ref> Designation as a Grade I [[listed building]] first took place in 1961.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=SHER21295/> A survey in 2002 found minor repairs were needed to the doors and wall plate.<ref name=garner/>

==Architecture==
[[File:Court Barn - geograph.org.uk - 567246.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|left|The barn showing the [[buttress]]es and (at top) [[Crosses in heraldry|croix pommée]] ventilation.]]
The rectangular five-bay barn is {{convert|50|ft}} long and {{convert|20|ft|6|in}} wide, although it was previously larger.<ref name=nhle/><ref>{{cite book|last1=May|first1=F.|title=Proceedings, Volumes 123-124|date=1980|publisher=Somersetshire Archaeological and Natural History Society|page=32}}</ref> The middle bay is slightly longer than the others because of the central [[porch]]es.<ref name=sher>{{cite web|title=Court Barn and dovecot, West Bradley|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/25350|website=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=24 May 2015}}</ref> The barn is built of local [[Blue Lias]] stone with some better quality [[Oolite|oolitic]] [[ashlar]] used for the [[quoin]]s on the corners and the porches which provided cover for goods being loaded and unloaded at the doors.<ref name=sher/> It is supported by two-stage [[buttress]]es reaching to three quarters of the height of the walls.<ref name=nhle/> Each of the side walls has ventilation slits, or breathers, with those in the end walls being in the shape of a [[Crosses in heraldry|croix pommée]].<ref name=radford79/><ref name=SHER21295>{{cite web|title=Court Barn, Scott's Lane (East side), West Bradley|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/21295|website=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=24 May 2015}}</ref> The barn originally had an attached [[dovecote]] on the western end,<ref name=radford79/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Pevsner|first1=Nikolaus|authorlink=Nikolaus Pevsner|title=South and West Somerset|date=1958|publisher=[[Penguin Books]]|page=336}}</ref> and still has niches for birds inside the barn and on the east gable wall.<ref name=nhle/> The dovecote was adapted into a calf shed.<ref name=nt/>

The roof was originally [[thatching|thatched]] but now is tiled, and is supported by [[cruck]] bracing to the [[Timber framing|timber frame]] of six principal [[truss]]es.<ref name=nhle/><ref name=nt/><ref name=radford79/> The design of the roof is similar to that in the other tithe barns of Glastonbury Abbey at [[Tithe Barn, Pilton|Pilton]], [[Tithe Barn, Manor Farm, Doulting|Manor Farm, Doulting]] and Glastonbury itself, which is now part of the [[Somerset Rural Life Museum]].<ref name=radford79/> The carriage porch where wagons would have been unloaded is covered by the sloping roof.<ref>{{cite web|title=Court Barn, West Bradley|url=https://www.greatbarns.org.uk/west_pennard_barn.html|publisher=Ken's Great Barns|access-date=24 May 2015}}</ref>

14191563.title: Stoke sub Hamdon Priory
14191563.extract:
Stoke sub Hamdon Priory is a complex of buildings and ruins which initially formed a 14th-century college for the chantry chapel of St Nicholas, and later was the site of a farm in Stoke-sub-Hamdon, Somerset, England. The only building remaining from the college is a great hall and attached dwelling, dating from the late 15th century. The hall is designated by English Heritage as a Grade I listed building, while the outbuildings and gateway are Grade II listed. The whole site has been scheduled as an ancient monument. A number of the farm buildings are in poor condition, and have been added to the Heritage at Risk Register.
The college was formed in 1304 as a chantry college, funded by John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp to serve the free chapel in his nearby manor house. Over the following 150 years, the college fell into disrepair and was rebuilt around 1460. During the dissolution, the land passed into the laity, and was a tenanted farm until the middle of the 20th century. The National Trust bought the property in 1946, and with the exception of the part of the house which is inhabited, the site is now open to the public. Despite being known as "The Priory", or "Stoke sub Hamdon Priory", the building has never been used as a priory, and there is no record of a monastic house in Stoke sub Hamdon.

{{Short description|Grade I listed building in Somerset, England}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Use British English|date=December 2024}} {{good article}} {{Infobox historic site |image = Stoke sub Hamdon Priory hall.jpg |caption = The north end of the house ''(left)'', and the attached great hall ''(right)'' at Stoke sub Hamdon Priory |name = Stoke sub Hamdon Priory |location = [[Stoke-sub-Hamdon]],
[[Somerset]], England |locmapin = Somerset |coordinates = {{coord|50.9545|-2.7488|display=inline,title}} | built = 1304 | built_for = [[John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp (first creation)|John de Beauchamp,
1st Baron Beauchamp]] | rebuilt = c. 1450–60 | restored = 1967 | owner = [[National Trust]] }} '''Stoke sub Hamdon Priory''' is a complex of buildings and ruins which initially formed a 14th-century college for the chantry chapel of St Nicholas, and later was the site of a farm in [[Stoke-sub-Hamdon]], [[Somerset]], England. The only building remaining from the college is a [[great hall]] and attached dwelling, dating from the late 15th century. The hall is designated by [[English Heritage]] as a Grade I [[Listed building (United Kingdom)|listed building]], while the outbuildings and gateway are Grade II listed. The whole site has been [[Scheduled monument|scheduled as an ancient monument]]. A number of the farm buildings are in poor condition, and have been added to the [[Heritage at Risk Register]]. The college was formed in 1304 as a [[chantry college]], funded by [[John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp (first creation)|John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp]] to serve the free chapel in his nearby manor house. Over the following 150 years, the college fell into disrepair and was rebuilt around 1460. During the dissolution, the land passed into the [[laity]], and was a tenanted farm until the middle of the 20th century. The [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] bought the property in 1946, and with the exception of the part of the house which is inhabited, the site is now open to the public. Despite being known as "The Priory", or "Stoke sub Hamdon Priory", the building has never been used as a [[priory]], and there is no record of a monastic house in Stoke sub Hamdon. ==History== Originally, a rectory was located on the site, which provided a home for the rector who officiated in the private chapel of St. Nicholas in the Beauchamp manor house nearby. When the rector, Henry de Wyk, resigned in 1304, the lord of the manor, [[John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp (first creation)|John de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Beauchamp]], established a [[chantry]] and founded a college for five chaplains.{{efn|"College" in this sense refers to a complex in which secular clergy lived, but without the strict confines of a monastic order.}}{{Cite book |last=Ireland |first=Phyllis |year=1971 |title=Archaeological properties in the County of Somerset |publisher=National Trust}} It is suggested in the [[English Heritage]] listing that the rectory was probably already owned by the Beauchamps, but if not they purchased it upon de Wyk's departure.{{National Heritage List for England |num=1020665 |desc=Medieval secular college at Parsonage Farm |access-date=5 April 2015}} The college was composed of four priests governed by a [[Provost (religion)|provost]], and was attached to the manor house chapel.{{Cite journal |last=Pantin |first=W. A. |author-link=William Abel Pantin |year=1959 |title=Chantry Priests' Houses and other Medieval Lodgings |journal=Medieval Archaeology |volume=3 |publisher=Society for Medieval Archaeology |url=http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archives/archiveDownload?t=arch-769-1/dissemination/pdf/vol03/3_216_258.pdf |pages=219–224 |doi=10.1080/00766097.1959.11735592 |access-date=16 December 2013}} A [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] report referenced in the Historic Environment Record could not determine if the pre-1304 rectory was retained for the college's use, or if a new building was erected instead.{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/54577 |title=Secular College, Parsonage Farm, Stoke sub Hamdon |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=16 December 2013}} In 1444, a report by the [[Bishop of Bath and Wells]], [[Thomas Beckington]], recorded that, due to poor management by the provost, the college had fallen into disrepair: the buildings were in a bad state, and only two priests remained alongside the provost, rather than the intended four. Beckington gave the governance of the college to the [[precentor]] of [[Wells, Somerset|Wells]], and a few years later the current building was erected. In his article, ''Chantry Priests' Houses and other Medieval Lodgings'', [[William Abel Pantin|W. A. Pantin]] suggests that this building is probably smaller than the original college, due to the reduced number of clergy, and that it was most likely erected around 1450–60. The English Heritage listing refers to the surviving building as being "apparently the Provost's Lodging."{{NHLE |desc=Parsonage Farmhouse The Priory |num=1260178 | |access-date=15 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}} From 1473 to 1508 Provost Coorte was in charge; however for 36 years during that time he was non-resident. {{multiple image | align = left |image1=The Priory - Stoke Sub Hamdon (3) - geograph.org.uk - 897576.jpg|caption1=Priory stable |image2=The old barn, Stoke sub Hamdon Priory - geograph.org.uk - 1380654.jpg|caption2=The old barn }} During the reign of [[Henry VIII of England|Henry VIII]] the chantry was under the control of the crown with Provosts Woulset and Carmer both being the kings chaplains and it unlikely that any investment was made in Stoke sub Hamdon Priory. By the time of the [[Chantry#Abolition of Chantries Acts, 1545 and 1547|dissolution]] in 1548, the chantry was already greatly reduced. The chantry holder, Thomas Canner, was also the parish priest, but performed his duties by deputy: he supplied one to carry out his parochial role, and another to perform his chantry duties. The college building had become a free chapel, and served as a [[chapel of ease]] for the village's residents, offering a convenient alternative to the parish church of [[Church of St Mary the Virgin, East Stoke|St Mary the Virgin]] which was a mile away in East Stoke. The Abolition of Chantries Act resulted in the college buildings being sold to the [[laity]] in 1548. The ownership of the estate exchanged hands frequently over the following 70 years, and during most of the period it was leased out to various tenants.{{Cite web |last1=Baggs |first1=A. P. |year=1974 |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=66503 |title=Parishes: Stoke sub Hamdon |work=A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 3 |pages=235–249 |editor=Dunning, R. W. |last2=Bush |first2=R. J. E. |last3=Tomlinson |first3=Margaret |access-date=17 December 2013}} The college was converted into a private house, and underwent significant renovation. Pantin suggests that the building work can be approximately dated to the period in which the Strode family inhabited the house, based upon an inscription in some panelling, "1585/TS", in which the TS stands for Thomas Strode. The building was also expanded on its south side, along the street. Over the subsequent three centuries, the estate was primarily passed on through marriage and inheritance within families, though it was sold a few times; primarily the ownership was held by the Robinsons, the Rodbards, and the Hawkesworths. None of the three families lived on the estate, which was at the time a farm worked by a string of lessees. In 1897 John William Bain Hawkesworth sold part of the holding, keeping just the house and some land. The farm was known as Parsonage Farm from the middle of the 19th century, and continued to be tended until around 1960. The property was purchased by the National Trust in 1946, and some restoration work was conducted in 1967. The complex of buildings was scheduled as an [[ancient monument]] in May 1951, and the former chantry house was listed as a Grade I building in April 1961. At the same time, the other buildings on site were listed as Grade II buildings: the gateway and wall,{{NHLE |desc=Gateway and Wall linking the Priory and the Barn, about 14 metres north |num=1242240 |access-date=22 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}} three barns (one of which is ruined),{{NHLE |desc=Barn about 14 metres north of the Priory |num=1260179 |access-date=22 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}}{{NHLE |desc=Barn about 25 metres north west of the Priory |num=1242150 |access-date=22 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}}{{NHLE |desc=Remains of barn about 15 metres west of the Priory |num=1260180 |access-date=24 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}} a ruined outbuilding and a dovecote.{{NHLE |desc=Barn Ruined building about 40 metres north west of the Priory |num=1260105 |access-date=22 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}}{{NHLE |desc=Dovecote about 50 metres west of the Priory |num=1242246 |access-date=22 December 2013|fewer-links=yes}} ==Architecture== [[File:Priory gateway - Stoke sub Hamdon - geograph.org.uk - 1556535.jpg|thumb|upright|The gateway]] The buildings are constructed from [[Hamstone]], a [[Jurassic]] [[limestone]] quarried on the local [[Ham Hill, Somerset|Ham Hill]]. The priory itself is linked to a barn by a wall. It includes a gateway which provides access from North Street. The {{convert|5|m|ft}} high wall dates from the 15th century and includes an arched gateway which has a [[buttress]] on its western side.{{cite web |title=Gateway and wall linking The Priory and the barn, about 14 metres north, North Street |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56421 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} The barn is largely from the 18th century; however it incorporates material from the former building. The southern end is supported by two buttresses and the north side includes a door on the first floor.{{cite web |title=Barn about 14 metres north of The Priory, North Road |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56422 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} The other barn which is about {{convert|25|m|ft}} north west of The Priory was built in the 15th century. It has partially [[Thatching|thatched]] roof,{{cite web |title=Barn about 25 metres north-west of The Priory, North Street |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56423 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} and served as a [[tithe barn]]. The other outbuilding which is about {{convert|40|m|ft}} north west of The Priory may once have been used as a wagon shed.{{cite web |title=Ruined building about 40 metres north-west of The Priory, North Street |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56424 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} A further 15th century barn to the west of The Priory is now ruined, following a fire in 1969.{{cite web |title=Remains of barn about 15 metres west of The Priory, North Street |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56425 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} It is close to the circular [[Dovecote]] which may date from the 14th century.{{cite web |title=Dovecote about 50 metres west of The Priory, North Street |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/56426 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=4 February 2014}} Pigeons and doves were an important food source historically kept for their eggs, flesh, and dung.{{Cite web |url=http://www.pigeoncote.com/dovecote/dovecote.html |title=Pigeoncote.com |publisher=Pigeoncote.com |access-date=30 December 2013}}{{Cite book |last=Wright |first=Geoffrey N. |year=2004 |title=Abbeys and Priories |publisher=Shire Publications Ltd |isbn=978-0747805892 |page=33 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lWAYvsIPbMwC&dq=Bruton+&pg=PA5 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The main priory building itself is of an L-shaped plan and consists of three unequal wings. The oldest part contains the hall, screens and dormitory. This was built in the 14th century but contains stones from the previous building, which show oblique tooling found in [[Norman architecture]]. The two-storey hall is {{convert|28|ft|m}} long and {{convert|18|ft|m}} wide. It was originally used as the refectory, with a window being added by Bishop Beckington in the 15th century, and later became a coal store. The hall also has arches into bays and an [[Ogee|ogee-headed]] recess which may have been an [[aumbry]]. At the eastern end of the hall is a parlour on the ground floor and, on the first floor, is a dormitory. The chapel next to the dormitory can be seen through a [[Hagioscope|squint]] which is unusually combined with a [[piscina]]. The central block south of the hall contains the dining room and kitchen on the ground floor with bedrooms above. Both have chamfered beams made of elm which are approximately {{convert|19|ft|m}} long. Centrally between the two rooms is a large medieval fireplace including a bread oven. Next to the kitchen is the large south store. ==See also== * [[Grade I listed buildings in South Somerset]] * [[List of National Trust properties in Somerset]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} ==References== {{reflist|33em}} ==External links== {{commons category|Stoke sub Hamdon Priory}} * [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/stoke-sub-hamdon-priory Stoke sub Hamdon Priory, National Trust] [[Category:Buildings and structures completed in 1304]] [[Category:Churches completed in the 1300s]] [[Category:Grade I listed buildings in South Somerset]] [[Category:National Trust properties in Somerset]] [[Category:Clergy houses in England]] [[Category:Scheduled monuments in South Somerset]] [[Category:Structures on the Heritage at Risk register in Somerset]] [[Category:Tourist attractions in Somerset]] [[Category:Grade I listed houses in Somerset]] [[Category:1304 establishments in England]]

22385695.title: Yarn Market, Dunster
22385695.extract:
The Yarn Market in Dunster, Somerset, England was built in the early 17th century. It has been designated as a Grade I listed building and scheduled monument. Dunster was an important market place in the Middle Ages particularly following the construction of Dunster Castle and the establishment of the Priory Church of St George.
The market cross was probably built in 1609 by the Luttrell family who were the local lords of the manor to maintain the importance of the village as a market, particularly for wool and cloth. It still bears the damage caused by cannon fire in the Civil War. Nearby was an older cross known as the Butter Cross which has subsequently been moved to the outskirts of the village. The Yarn Market is an octagonal building constructed around a central pier. The tiled roof provides shelter from the rain.

The '''Yarn Market''' in [[Dunster]], [[Somerset]], England was built in the early 17th century. It has been designated as a Grade I [[listed building]] and [[scheduled monument]].<ref name="IoE">{{NHLE |num=1173428 |desc=Yarn Market |access-date=28 August 2007}}</ref><ref name=nhlesched>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1015706 |desc=The Yarn Market|access-date=5 April 2015}}</ref> Dunster was an important market place in the [[Middle Ages]] particularly following the construction of [[Dunster Castle]] and the establishment of the [[Priory Church of St George, Dunster|Priory Church of St George]].

The [[market cross]] was probably built in 1609 by the [[Earl of Carhampton|Luttrell family]] who were the local [[Lord of the manor|lords of the manor]] to maintain the importance of the village as a market, particularly for wool and cloth. It still bears the damage caused by cannon fire in the [[English Civil War|Civil War]]. Nearby was an older cross known as the [[Dunster Butter Cross|Butter Cross]] which has subsequently been moved to the outskirts of the village. The Yarn Market is an octagonal building constructed around a central [[Pier (architecture)|pier]]. The tiled roof provides shelter from the rain.

==History==
[[Dunster Castle]] stands on a site which has been fortified since the late [[Anglo-Saxon]] period, signifying the importance of the area.<ref name=gathercole/> After the [[Norman conquest of England]] in the 11th century, [[William de Moyon|William de Mohun]] constructed a timber castle on the site as part of the pacification of Somerset.<ref>Prior, Stuart. (2006) ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=vuqjAAAACAAJ The Norman Art of War: a Few Well-Positioned Castles.]'' Stroud, UK: Tempus. {{ISBN|0-7524-3651-1}}.</ref>

A stone [[shell keep]] was built on the motte by the start of the 12th century, and the castle survived a siege during the early years of [[the Anarchy]]. At the end of the 14th century the de Mohuns sold the castle to the [[Earl of Carhampton|Luttrell family]].<ref>Garnett, Oliver. (2003) ''Dunster Castle, Somerset.''London: The National Trust. {{ISBN|978-1-84359-049-1}}. pages 38-39</ref>

Dunster had become a centre for woollen and clothing production by the 13th century, with the market dating back to at least 1222, and a particular kind of kersey or broadcloth became known as 'Dunsters'.<ref name=gathercole>{{cite web|url=http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/Somerset_EUS_Dunster.pdf |title=Dunster |last=Gathercole |first=Clare |work=The Somerset Urban Archaeological Survey |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=6 June 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131225020003/http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/Somerset_EUS_Dunster.pdf |archive-date=25 December 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=1133|title=Yarn Market Dunster|publisher=Everything Exmoor|access-date=21 January 2015|archive-date=17 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817220050/http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=1133|url-status=dead}}</ref> The prosperity of Dunster was based on the wool trade, with profits helping to pay for the construction of the tower of the [[Priory Church of St George, Dunster|Priory Church of St George]] and provide other amenities. By the 15th century the importance of the town was declining particularly due to the silting up of the harbour.<ref name=gathercole/> The Luttrells wanted to maintain the town's importance as a market, and in 1609 George Luttrell, of the [[Earl of Carhampton|Luttrell family]] constructed the market to shelter traders and their wares from the rain and provide more security for their wares.<ref name=gathercole/><ref>{{cite web|title=Yarn Market — History and Research|url=http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/daysout/properties/dunster-yarn-market/history-and-research/|publisher=English Heritage|access-date=6 June 2014}}</ref> The exact date of construction is debated and a variety of dates are given in different sources, however 1609 is considered the most likely.<ref name=nhlesched/><ref name=gathercole/>

A second market cross, known as the [[Dunster Butter Cross|Butter Cross]], which was built in the 15th century used to stand near the Yarn Market but was moved to the outskirts of the village in the 18th or 19th century.<ref name="IoE" /><ref name="nhlesched" /><ref>{{cite news|title=The Butter Cross at Dunster|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000528/19420926/024/0004|access-date=7 July 2014|work=Taunton Courier, and Western Advertiser|date=26 September 1942| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Yarn Market is in the guardianship of [[English Heritage]] but is managed by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/34962|title=Yarn Market, High Street (West side), Dunster|work=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=26 May 2009}}</ref> In 1951 the [[Ministry of Works (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Works]] took over various properties including the Yarn Market from the [[Crown Estate]]. They carried out restoration works, however this was controversial as the shape of the roof was changed to more closely resemble the appearance of the original building, rather than that produced by subsequent revisions.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Chapple|first1=Nick|title=A History of the National Heritage Collection. Volume Six: 1945-1953|url=http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/036_2014WEB.pdf|publisher=English Heritage|access-date=19 September 2015|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304065643/http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/036_2014WEB.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Architecture==
[[File:Roof of Yarn Market Dunster.JPG|thumb|left|View of the supporting structure of the roof]]
The [[octagon]]al building, which is {{convert|9.4|m}} in diameter, has a central stone [[Pier (architecture)|pier]] which supports a heavy timber framework for the structure.<ref>{{cite book|title=Heritage Unlocked|date=2004|publisher=English Heritage|isbn=1850748756|page=66}}</ref> The [[slate]] roof has a central wooden [[Roof lantern|lantern]] topped by a [[weather vane]].<ref name="IoE"/> The roof is interrupted by a series of [[dormer]] windows.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Patrick|title=Buildings of Britain 1550-1750: South West England|year=1981|publisher=Moorland|isbn=0861900308|pages=100–101}}</ref> Around the periphery is a low wall and vertical timber supports.<ref name="nhle">{{National Heritage List for England|num=1173428|desc=Yarn Market|access-date=5 April 2015}}</ref> Some of the sills are stone and others timber.<ref name=nhlesched/>

One of the roof beams has a hole in it, a result of cannon fire in the [[English Civil War|Civil War]], when [[Dunster Castle]] was a besieged Royalist stronghold for five months under the command of Colonel Wyndham.<ref name="dunsthist">{{cite web|url=http://www.dunstertithebarn.org.uk/history-dunster.htm|title=Brief History of Dunster|publisher=Dunster Tithe Barn|access-date=26 May 2009|archive-date=20 November 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081120215318/http://www.dunstertithebarn.org.uk/history-dunster.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Following the damage, it was restored in 1647 to its present condition by [[Francis Luttrell (1628–1666)|Francis Luttrell]].<ref name=nhlesched/>

The building was the inspiration for the Rest House, on [[Bournville]] Village Green in Birmingham, which was built in 1914 to commemorate the silver wedding anniversary of [[George Cadbury|George]] and [[Elizabeth Cadbury]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bournvillecarillon.co.uk/resthouse|title=History of the Rest House|website=Bournville Carillion}}</ref>
